title: Emotional drivers of misinformation consumption and toxicity on YouTube
screen_reason: The paper's aim is emotional/toxicity analysis, not prevalence, but its dataset breakdown (Table 1) gives verbatim counts with a common denominator for the share of a COVID-19 YouTube corpus coming from questionable (misinformation) channels, for the share of comments posted on those channels, and for the share of commenters classified as misinformation-prone (stated verbatim as 2.9%). Under R8 an exact part/whole share from verbatim counts with the same denominator is keepable, and under the rule that a study with another aim is still included if a descriptive share is reported anywhere, this is eligible.

estimates.measure_type: % of Italian YouTube COVID-19 videos in the corpus that were posted by channels labelled questionable (regularly producing unverified or false content)
estimates.denominator: 30,436 Italian YouTube videos about SARS-CoV-2 retrieved by keyword search (coronavirus, nCov, corona virus, corona-virus, covid, SARS-CoV) via the YouTube Data API, posted 1 December 2019 to 21 April 2020, from 7,157 channels
estimates.definition: A video counts if the channel that posted it appears on the curated questionable list, i.e. a channel that regularly produced unverified or false content or was affiliated with news outlets that had repeatedly failed independent fact-checks
estimates.misinfo_def: "A channel was labeled as questionable if it regularly produced unverified or false content, or was affiliated with news outlets that had repeatedly failed fact-checks conducted by independent organizations."
estimates.source_quote: Table 1 Breakdown of the YouTube dataset. Trustworthiness Channels Videos Comments Users Reliable 7,140 29,975 1,170,461 304,586 Questionable 17 464 103,475 9,094 Undefined – – – 10,326 Total 7,157 30,436 1,273,930 324,006
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Channel-level reliability labels inherited from Cinelli et al. (2021), based on curated lists compiled from assessments by fact-checking and media-rating platforms active in Italy: bufale.net, butac.it, facta.news, newsguardtech.com and pagellapolitica.it. All channels not on those lists were labelled reliable. No per-video coding and no inter-rater reliability reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: Data was collected using the official YouTube Data application programming interface (API), by performing a keyword search for videos that matched a list of keywords, i.e., coronavirus, nCov, corona virus, corona-virus, covid, SARS-CoV.
estimates.notes: 464/30,436 = 1.52%, an exact part/whole share from two verbatim counts in the same table row set (R8-compliant). Only 17 of 7,157 channels (0.24%) were on the questionable list; because 'reliable' is defined residually (everything not on a curated Italian questionable list), this share is bounded from above by the coverage of those lists and should be read as a lower bound. The paper itself never states this percentage, so it is a derived-but-permitted part/whole.

estimates.measure_type: % of Italian YouTube COVID-19 comments that were posted on videos from questionable (misinformation) channels
estimates.value_raw: 103,475 comments on questionable channels of 1,273,930 total comments (Table 1)
estimates.denominator: 1,273,930 Italian-language YouTube comments on SARS-CoV-2 videos, posted 15 January 2020 to 15 June 2020 by 324,006 users
estimates.definition: A comment counts if the video it was posted on belongs to a channel on the curated questionable list
estimates.misinfo_def: "A channel was labeled as questionable if it regularly produced unverified or false content, or was affiliated with news outlets that had repeatedly failed fact-checks conducted by independent organizations."
estimates.source_quote: Table 1 Breakdown of the YouTube dataset. Trustworthiness Channels Videos Comments Users Reliable 7,140 29,975 1,170,461 304,586 Questionable 17 464 103,475 9,094 Undefined – – – 10,326 Total 7,157 30,436 1,273,930 324,006
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same channel-level curated Italian reliability lists (bufale.net, butac.it, facta.news, newsguardtech.com, pagellapolitica.it) inherited from Cinelli et al. (2021).
estimates.moderator_quote: We used data employed in Cinelli et al. (2021), which consists of about 1.3 million Italian comments to videos about SARS-CoV-2 posted on YouTube. [...] The set of videos covers the time window that goes from 01/12/2019 to 21/04/2020, while the set of comments ranges in the time window that goes from 15/01/2020 to 15/06/2020.
estimates.notes: 103,475/1,273,930 = 8.12%, an exact part/whole share from verbatim table counts (R8-compliant). borderline=true on the construct: the denominator is user-generated engagement items (comments), and the misinformation label attaches to the video/channel the comment sits under, not to the comment itself. Coded SHARING/content_share under the rule that engagement denominators map to SHARING; an adjudicator could argue for EXPOSURE (diet_share), since comments proxy attention to questionable sources rather than the resharing of misinformation. Notably the engagement share (8.1%) is five times the supply share (1.5% of videos), which is itself an informative asymmetry.

estimates.measure_type: % of classified Italian YouTube COVID-19 commenters who were misinformation-prone (at least 75% of their comments on questionable channels)
estimates.value_raw: 96.8% of users have a defined leaning, of which 2.9% is classified as misinformation-prone (9,094 of 313,680 users)
estimates.denominator: 313,680 users with a defined leaning (96.8% of the 324,006 users who commented on the COVID-19 video corpus; the remaining 3.2% had an intermediate leaning and were left Undefined)
estimates.definition: A user is misinformation-prone if the proportion of their comments posted on questionable channels is in [0.75, 1]; mainstream-prone if in [0, 0.25]
estimates.misinfo_def: "A channel was labeled as questionable if it regularly produced unverified or false content, or was affiliated with news outlets that had repeatedly failed fact-checks conducted by independent organizations."
estimates.source_quote: Users with lu in the intermediate range ð0:25; 0:75Þ remain Undefined, representing 3.2% of the total. Consequently, 96.8% of users have a defined leaning, of which 2.9% is classified as misinformation-prone.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same channel-level curated Italian reliability lists inherited from Cinelli et al. (2021); user leaning computed as the proportion of a user's comments posted on questionable channels.
estimates.moderator_quote: To assign the label indicating the category of a user u, the leaning statistic lu was computed as the proportion of comments posted on questionable channels [...] This classification captures commenting preferences only, without making assumptions about users' agreement with the content.
estimates.notes: JUDGEMENT CALL: this is an actor share, but NOT the usual 'share of users who engaged with misinformation at least once' - the threshold is at least 75% of a user's comments on questionable channels, so it is much stricter than 'any' and will read far lower than a comparable 'any exposure' actor share. Coded SHARING/actor_share with borderline=true; an adjudicator may prefer to drop it as not comparable to other actor shares. The verbatim 2.9% matches Table 1 (9,094 questionable-leaning users / (304,586 + 9,094) = 2.90%) and 3.2% matches 10,326/324,006. NOTE A PAPER-INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY: Table 2 reports 'N. users 304,586 = 295,492 MAp + 9,094 MIp' at threshold 0, which contradicts Table 1 where 304,586 is the count of reliable-leaning (MAp) users alone; the text's 2.9%/3.2% figures are consistent with Table 1, not with Table 2.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) The channel-level share (17 of 7,157 channels = 0.24% questionable) is a fourth possible CONTENT row with a different unit; not extracted separately because it duplicates the video-level row's information and the tiny questionable-channel count (17) is an artifact of the curated list's coverage rather than a measured prevalence. (2) '705,856 comments (55.4%) contain at least one basic emotion' is an emotion-detection share, not a misinformation share. (3) All emotion probabilities, chi-square/Cramer's V statistics (Table 4), SHAP results, arborescence values and '25% greater emotional diversity' are within-group comparative statistics about emotions, not prevalence. (4) Model performance figures in Table 3 (accuracy, precision, F1) are classifier metrics for the random forest used to explain emotional features, not prevalence estimates. (5) The toxicity distribution is described only qualitatively ('The majority of comments are deemed acceptable') with no numbers, and toxicity is in any case not a misinformation construct. (6) 'around 24 million Italians - roughly one third of the population - used YouTube in 2019' and the 1%-rule estimate of 240k active users are cited background statistics, not this study's own measurements.

rob.design: Secondary analysis of the Cinelli et al. (2021) corpus: Italian-language YouTube videos about SARS-CoV-2 retrieved by keyword search through the official YouTube Data API (videos 1 December 2019 - 21 April 2020; comments 15 January - 15 June 2020), giving 7,157 channels, 30,436 videos, 1,273,930 comments and 324,006 users. Misinformation is measured at the CHANNEL level from curated Italian fact-checking and media-rating lists (bufale.net, butac.it, facta.news, newsguardtech.com, pagellapolitica.it), with everything not on those lists treated as reliable; no per-item veracity coding, no inter-coder reliability, and no precision/recall for the labelling. Toxicity labels come from a hate-speech detection model, also inherited. The corpus is a keyword-defined convenience sample of one topic on one platform in one country; commenters are self-selected and are not a sample of the Italian public. The paper reports no response rate (behavioural data) and no reliability statistics for the misinformation labels.
rob.item6_quote: Building on the approach proposed in Cinelli et al. (2021), each comment c was assigned a label—reliable or questionable—based on the classification of the YouTube channel it appeared on. [...] A channel was labeled as questionable if it regularly produced unverified or false content, or was affiliated with news outlets that had repeatedly failed fact-checks conducted by independent organizations. The labeling was based on curated lists compiled using assessments from fact-checking and media-rating platforms active in Italy, including bufale.net, butac.it, facta.news, newsguardtech.com, and pagellapolitica.it. All remaining channels were labeled as reliable.
